angle: stakes hook: players say your 90% shot is rigged (HookText: 90% to hit, missed twice); rule out broken dice: two misses in a row is 1 in 100, and in 100 shots 6 players in 10 see it; nobody feels 1 in 100; fix: roll two numbers 0-99 and average them, hit if the average is under 90; now 90% really hits 98% and a double miss is 1 in 2,770; re-hook: the enemy's long shots: 10% lands 2%, 50% stays a coin flip; payoff: two dice pile up in the middle, the number on screen lies in your favor; Fire Emblem since 2002; CTA: checkable question (80% -> 92%)
title: Why a 90% hit in Fire Emblem is really 98%
description:
Players remember misses: at an honest 90%, two misses in a row happen 1 time in 100, and in 100 shots about 6 players in 10 see it happen. So roll two random numbers from 0 to 99 and hit if their average is under the shown rate. Averages pile up in the middle, so a shown 90% really hits 98.1% of the time (a double miss becomes 1 in 2,770), a shown 10% lands 2.1%, and 50% stays about a coin flip. Fire Emblem has used this "true hit" since The Binding Blade (2002, Game Boy Advance).

Numbers checked in code (exact counts over all 10,000 pairs of rolls, plus 1,000,000-shot simulations). Sources: https://fireemblemwiki.org/wiki/True_hit https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Emblem:_The_Binding_Blade

beats.say: Players say your 90% shot is rigged.
Your dice are fine. Two misses in a row is one in 100.
And in 100 shots, 6 players in 10 see it happen. Nobody remembers the hits.
So stop rolling one number. Roll two, from 0 to 99, and average them.
The shot hits if the average is under 90.
Now your 90% shot hits 98% of the time. Two misses in a row: one in 2,770.
But that's only half the trick. Watch the enemy's long shots.
Their 10% shot now lands just 2% of the time. A 50% shot stays a coin flip.
Two dice pile up in the middle, so good odds get better and bad odds get worse.
The number on screen lies, in your favor. Fire Emblem has done this since 2002.
So if the screen says 80%, how often does it really hit?
